title: Lab Practice
summary: The applied side of the course, drawn from the first three assignments — which the test announcement puts on the syllabus alongside the lectures. The questions here are about the *method*: how an experiment is set up, why the test set is quarantined, and how to read the results it produces. Not about the steps of any particular notebook.

keyFacts.definition: Every random step — the split, the shuffle, the model's own randomness — takes a fixed `random_state`, so a rerun gives the same numbers and any change in the result is attributable to the change in the method rather than to a different split.
`stratify=y` on `train_test_split` preserves the class proportions of `y` in every part. It matters most when the classes are imbalanced or the dataset is small.

subtopics.title: The experimental workflow
subtopics.summary: The shape every supervised experiment shares: load, clean, split, scale, fit, evaluate — with the test set held back until the very end.

keyFacts.term: Why the test set is quarantined
keyFacts.definition: Any data used to *choose* a model stops being an unbiased estimate of performance on new data. Selecting on the test set optimises against it, so its score becomes optimistic.
60/20/20 train/validation/test, achieved by two calls: `test_size=0.2` to peel off the test set, then `test_size=0.25` on the remainder (25% of 80% = 20%).

questions.prompt: Explain, in 2–3 sentences, why the test set should not be used during model selection.
questions.answer:
The test set exists to estimate performance on **unseen** data. If you use it to choose between models, you are optimising against it, and it is no longer unseen — the winning model is partly winning by fitting that particular sample.

The reported test score then becomes **optimistic**, and the model may do noticeably worse in reality. Selection belongs on the **validation** set (or via cross-validation on the training data), leaving the test set untouched for a single final measurement.

questions.prompt: Why fix `random_state` on every random step of an experiment — the split, the shuffle, the model's own randomness?
questions.answer:
For **reproducibility**. Rerunning the code produces exactly the same splits and therefore the same numbers, so the results in the write-up match the code that produced them.

Without it every rerun gives slightly different accuracies, and there is then no way to tell a real effect of a change you made from the noise of a different split. With the seed fixed, any difference you observe is attributable to the change.

The seed also has to be **recorded**, not merely set — otherwise the run is repeatable only on your machine.

questions.prompt: An experiment repeats a train/validation split 30 times, using `random_state = seed + i` for i = 0…29. Why vary the seed rather than reusing one?
options: A fixed seed would give the same split every time, so all 30 repeats would be identical
Varying the seed makes the splits stratified
It increases the size of the training set each round
It is required before the results can be plotted
questions.explanation: The point of repeating is to see the **spread** of accuracies across different splits. With one seed there would be no spread to see — 30 copies of the same number.

questions.prompt: What does `stratify=y` do in `train_test_split`, and what goes wrong without it?
questions.answer:
It makes the split **preserve the class proportions** of `y` in every part. If the full data is 65% benign, both the train and the test set come out about 65% benign.

Without it the split is a plain random draw, so the proportions wander — and the smaller the dataset and the rarer the minority class, the further they can wander. In the bad case a class ends up thin in the training half, so the model barely learns it, and thin in the test half, so the score for it is measured on a handful of rows and is mostly noise.

questions.prompt: When does `stratify=y` matter most?
options: A small dataset with imbalanced classes
A large dataset with balanced classes
Any regression problem
Only when the model is kNN
questions.explanation: With plenty of data and balanced classes a random split is already close to stratified. The risk is a small, imbalanced dataset, where an unlucky draw can leave the minority class badly under-represented — or nearly absent — in the training half.

questions.prompt: You want a 60/20/20 train/validation/test split from two calls to `train_test_split`. The first peels off the test set with `test_size=0.2`. What `test_size` must the second call use on the remainder to leave 20% of the original as validation? Give it as a decimal.

steps.text: After the first split, `1 − 0.2 = 0.8` of the data remains.
You need 0.2 of the **original** out of that 0.8, so the fraction is `0.2 / 0.8`.

questions.explanation: The classic slip is passing 0.2 again, which gives 64/16/20 rather than 60/20/20.

questions.prompt: A `StandardScaler` is fitted with `.fit(X_train)` and then used to transform both the training and the test set. Why not fit it on all the data?
questions.answer:
Fitting on everything would let the **test set's mean and standard deviation** influence the transformation applied to the training data — information from data the model is not supposed to have seen. That is **data leakage**, and it makes the test score optimistic.

The scaler is fitted on the training data only, then that same fitted transformation is applied to the test data.

questions.prompt: Should the scaler be fitted before or after the train/test split?
options: After — fit on the training set only, then transform both
Before — so both sets are on the same scale
It makes no difference
Before, but only for kNN

questions.prompt: Wrapping the scaler and the model in a `Pipeline` — what problem does that solve?
questions.answer:
```python
Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler()),
          ("logistic", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
```

The pipeline's `fit` fits the scaler **on the training data only** and then the model, and its `predict` applies the *already fitted* scaler before predicting. Leakage from the held-out data becomes structurally impossible rather than something you have to remember.

It matters most when many models are fitted in a loop, or inside cross-validation, where a hand-applied scaler is easy to fit on the wrong rows without noticing.

questions.prompt: Put a standard supervised-learning experiment in order, from raw file to reported result.
questions.answer:
1. **Load** the data.
2. **Explore** — `info()`, `describe()`, a pairplot; identify problems.
3. **Clean** — drop identifier columns, handle missing values.
4. **Separate** X (predictors) from y (target).
5. **Split** — train/test, or train/validation/test, stratified, with a fixed seed.
6. **Scale**, fitting on the training data only.
7. **Fit** the model.
8. **Evaluate** — confusion matrix, classification report.
9. **Experiment** — vary the hyperparameter, plot, interpret.

The ordering that matters most is **split before scale**, and **test set last**.

questions.prompt: Which of these orderings leaks information from the test set?
options: Scale the whole dataset, then split
Split, then fit the scaler on train and transform both
Split, then fit a separate pipeline per subset
Split, then evaluate on the test set once at the end
questions.explanation: The scaler's mean and standard deviation would be computed partly from the test rows, so the training transformation carries information about data the model should not have seen.

questions.prompt: What is the term for information from held-out data reaching the training process — by scaling, imputing or selecting features before the split?
questions.hint: It names the direction the information travels, not the step that causes it.
questions.explanation: Every instance has the same shape: a quantity computed from rows the model is not supposed to have seen ends up influencing what it learns, so the held-out score is optimistic.

questions.prompt: Model selection happens on the {{1}} set; the {{2}} set is used once, at the end, to estimate real performance.
A dataset has {{n}} rows and is split 60/20/20 into train, validation and test. Roughly how many rows end up in the test set?

steps.text: The test set is 20% of the whole dataset: `{{n}} / 5`.
`= {{n / 5}}`, which need not be a whole number of rows.
`train_test_split` rounds the test side up, so take the nearest whole row: **{{round(n/5)}}**.

questions.explanation: Worth doing before quoting any accuracy: on a validation set this size, one percentage point is only a handful of examples.

subtopics.title: kNN in practice
subtopics.summary: Preparing data for a distance-based model, and what the choice of k actually trades off.

keyFacts.definition: An arbitrary id carries no signal but still contributes a full dimension to every distance, pushing genuinely similar examples apart. Drop it before fitting any distance-based model.

Small k is low bias and high variance — it follows individual points, noise included. Large k is high bias and low variance — it smooths toward the majority class. The best k is found on a validation set, never on the test set.

questions.prompt: Why should an `id` column be dropped before training, and why does it matter especially for kNN?
questions.answer:
It is an **arbitrary identifier** with no relationship to the target. Keeping it feeds the model pure noise.

For **kNN specifically** it is actively harmful: id values are large compared with the real predictors, so even after scaling the column still contributes a full dimension of meaningless distance, pushing genuinely similar examples apart.

A pairplot makes the case visible — an identifier shows no clustering by class in any panel.

questions.prompt: In a cancer-screening classifier where the positive class is malignant, are the two kinds of error equally costly? What follows for the choice of metric?
questions.answer:
They are **not** equally costly.

A **false negative** — a malignant tumour classified benign — is a missed cancer. A **false positive** leads to further testing that turns out negative: unpleasant and expensive, but recoverable.

So **recall on the malignant class matters more than precision**, and the decision threshold should be moved toward catching more positives even at the cost of more false alarms. Reporting accuracy alone hides which of the two the model is getting wrong.

questions.prompt: Every predictor in a dataset is already on the same 1–10 scale. Does standardisation still matter for kNN?
questions.answer:
Much less than usual — the features are already comparable, so no single one can dominate the distance the way a feature ranging to 1,000,000 would.

But it is not pointless: standardisation also equalises the **spread** of each feature, and features sharing a range need not share a variance. A feature that in practice only ever takes 1 or 2 contributes far less than one that uses the full range, and standardising evens that out.

The honest answer is the *reasoning* either way, not the ritual — and it changes completely the moment one column is on a different scale.

questions.prompt: Why do very small and very large values of k behave differently in kNN?
questions.answer:
**Very small k** (k = 1): the prediction comes from a single nearest point, so the model follows individual training examples including noisy and mislabelled ones. High variance, low bias — it **overfits**, and accuracy is unstable between splits.

**Very large k**: the neighbourhood covers a large part of the data, so predictions get smoothed toward the overall majority class. Low variance, high bias — it **underfits**, and as k approaches the dataset size every query returns the same answer.

The best k sits between: large enough to average away noise, small enough to keep local structure.

questions.prompt: Sweeping k upward from 1 and plotting accuracy, what shape does the curve usually take?
options: Rises quickly from k = 1, peaks over a broad range of small-to-moderate k, then declines slowly
Rises steadily, so the largest k tried is always the best
Falls monotonically from k = 1
Stays flat throughout
questions.explanation: The bias–variance trade-off drawn out: k = 1 is high variance, very large k is high bias, and the useful region is the broad plateau between them. The peak is usually flat enough that several values of k are indistinguishable.

questions.prompt: A k-sweep is evaluated on the **test** set and the best-scoring k is reported. What is the methodological problem, and how would you fix it?
questions.answer:
Choosing k by test-set accuracy is **selecting on the test set**. The reported accuracy for the winning k is then optimistic, because that k was picked partly for fitting this particular sample — the more values of k you tried, the more optimistic it is.

The fix is to sweep k on a **validation** set, or by cross-validation on the training data, pick the best k there, and only then measure the chosen model once on the test set.

A 60/20/20 split is set up to do exactly this.
questions.source: Lab 1 · Part 3; Lab 2 · Part 1; Lab 3 · setup

questions.prompt: Name two things you would look for in a raw dataset that could affect model performance, why each matters, and a fix for each.
questions.answer:
**1. Missing values.** *Why:* most estimators cannot fit with NaNs at all, and a distance is undefined if a coordinate is missing. *Fix:* drop the affected rows when they are a small fraction, otherwise impute — median for numeric, most frequent for categorical, fitted on the training data only.

**2. Columns that carry no signal.** Identifiers, row numbers, anything constant. *Why:* pure noise, and for distance-based models a large-magnitude id actively distorts the geometry. *Fix:* drop them.

**3. Class imbalance.** *Why:* accuracy becomes misleading — a majority-class-always model can score well — and an unlucky split can leave the minority class thin. *Fix:* stratify the split, and read per-class precision and recall rather than accuracy.

**4. Features on wildly different scales.** *Why:* they dominate distances and distort gradient descent. *Fix:* standardise, fitting the scaler on the training set.

questions.prompt: Why might dropping weakly-informative features improve a kNN classifier, and how would you spot candidates to drop?
questions.answer:
**Why it helps:** kNN weights every feature equally in the distance. A feature carrying little signal still contributes its full share of distance, so it dilutes the contribution of the informative ones and can change which points count as nearest. Removing it sharpens the neighbourhood — the dimensionality-reduction argument, applied where it bites hardest.

**How to spot candidates:** a pairplot or per-feature histograms split by class. A feature whose class distributions overlap almost completely separates nothing; one whose classes sit in different places carries signal.

**The caveat:** 'looks weak alone' is not the same as 'useless' — a feature can be uninformative on its own and useful in combination. Judge the subset by validation accuracy, not by the plot alone.

questions.prompt: Why does an irrelevant feature hurt kNN more than it hurts a linear model?
questions.answer:
A linear model can drive the irrelevant feature's coefficient toward zero and effectively ignore it — and regularisation pushes it to do exactly that.

kNN has no coefficients. **Every feature contributes equally to the distance**, so an irrelevant dimension adds noise to every neighbour calculation and can change which points come out nearest. There is no mechanism inside the method to down-weight it.

That is why feature selection and dimensionality reduction pay off most for distance-based methods, and why they degrade fastest as the number of features grows.
questions.source: Lab 1 · Part 3; c2 · slide 10; intro · slide 18

questions.prompt: A dataset has an identifier column, some missing values, and features on very different scales. Which of these is safe to do **before** the train/test split?
options: Dropping the identifier column
Fitting the scaler
Computing the median used to fill the missing values
Ranking the features by how well they separate the classes
questions.explanation: Dropping a column that carries no information is a decision about the *schema*, not a quantity learned from the rows, so it is safe either side of the split. Everything else in the list is **fitted** from data — a mean, a median, a ranking — and must be computed on the training half only, or it leaks.

questions.prompt: In kNN, k = 1 has high {{1}} and low {{2}}; very large k has the reverse.
questions.explanation: k is the complexity dial: small k is a flexible model that follows individual points, large k is a rigid one that smooths toward the majority.

questions.prompt: Which of these belong in the preparation of a dataset for kNN?
options: Dropping identifier columns
Handling missing values
Fitting the scaler on the training data only
Choosing k by test-set accuracy
questions.explanation: The fourth is the one to avoid: k is a hyperparameter, so it is chosen on validation data. Selecting it on the test set makes the reported test score optimistic.

subtopics.title: Tree complexity and model selection
subtopics.summary: Repeated splits, a geometric complexity sweep, and what the resulting spread actually tells you.

keyFacts.definition: A complexity parameter is swept in powers of two — 2, 4, 8 … 32768 — rather than in equal steps, so a handful of fits covers several orders of magnitude and each step is about equally informative.

keyFacts.term: Mean and standard deviation across repeats
keyFacts.definition: Repeating a split many times gives each setting a mean accuracy and a standard deviation. The mean says how good the setting is; the standard deviation says how much that depends on which split it got — how stable it is.

questions.prompt: What does `max_leaf_nodes` control, and how does it relate to model complexity?
questions.answer:
The **maximum number of leaf regions** the tree may split the space into. Each leaf holds one constant prediction.

More leaves means **more, smaller regions** — a more complex model, with more capacity to fit the training data and more risk of overfitting. It is the same complexity dial as `max_depth`, but counted in regions rather than levels.

questions.prompt: An experiment repeats a train/validation split {{r}} times and, for each split, trains one model per candidate value of a hyperparameter with {{v}} candidates. How many model fits is that?

steps.text: For every split, one model is trained per candidate value.
`{{r}} splits × {{v}} values`
`= {{r * v}}` fits.

questions.explanation: 450 fits — which is why the results go into a DataFrame to be aggregated rather than being printed as they go. It is also why the cost of a repeated experiment has to be estimated before starting one.

questions.prompt: Why sweep `max_leaf_nodes` in powers of two rather than in equal steps?
questions.answer:
The interesting behaviour spans **orders of magnitude**. Stepping linearly — 2, 4, 6, 8 … — would spend every trial in the tiny-tree region and never reach the overfitting end.

A geometric sweep covers 2 to 32768 in fifteen fits, and the effect of doubling capacity is roughly constant across the range, so each step is about equally informative.

questions.prompt: Why repeat a validation experiment 30 times rather than once?
questions.answer:
A single split gives a single number, and that number is partly luck — which examples happened to land in validation.

Thirty repeats give a **distribution**: you can see the **mean** performance of each setting *and* how **variable** it is. Only the second of those tells you whether a setting is unexpectedly unstable, and a single run can never show it.

questions.prompt: What does a violin plot of repeated results convey that a plot of the means does not?
questions.answer:
A violin plot shows the **full distribution** of the repeated accuracies for each setting: its **spread**, its **shape**, and where the density is concentrated. The width at any height is how common that accuracy was.

What a mean alone hides:
- the **variance** — two settings can share a mean while one is far less reliable
- **skew** — a long tail of bad splits pulling the mean down
- **bimodality** — two clusters of outcomes, which a mean reports as a value that never actually occurred

questions.prompt: Which feature of the results is visible in a violin plot but not in a plot of the means?
options: The spread and shape of the distribution
Which setting scored highest on average
The number of settings tested
The order of the settings

questions.prompt: Repeated splits give each setting a mean accuracy and a standard deviation. Which of those answers 'which settings are unexpectedly unstable'?
options: The standard deviation across the repeats
The mean accuracy
The difference between the mean and the standard deviation
Neither — stability can only be seen in a violin plot
questions.explanation: A high standard deviation means the setting's performance depends heavily on which split it got — the definition of unstable. The mean says how good it is, not how reliably.

questions.prompt: Would you expect `max_leaf_nodes = 2` or `max_leaf_nodes = 32768` to have the higher variance across splits? Explain.
questions.answer:
**32768** — the large tree.

A 2-leaf tree makes one split; there is very little to vary, so it gives a consistently mediocre result across every split. That is **low variance, high bias**.

A 32768-leaf tree fits the fine structure of whichever training sample it was given, and that structure differs between splits — so its validation accuracy moves around much more. **High variance**, which is exactly c2's 'unstable classifier' point measured empirically.
questions.source: Lab 2 · Part 2; c2 · slide 14; c3 · slide 26

questions.prompt: Would a validation curve averaged over many repeated splits and a single test-set curve recommend the same model? Why might they differ?
questions.answer:
They usually recommend a **similar** setting, but rarely the exact same one.

Reasons they can differ:
- The validation curve is averaged over many splits of a *subset* of the training data; the test curve comes from **one** model fitted on all of it. More training data can shift the best complexity **upward**.
- The test set is a **single sample**, so its curve carries its own noise — a difference of a fraction of a percent between adjacent settings is not meaningful.

Whether the disagreement matters depends on the **size** of the gap: if the two candidates are within the noise of each other, either is fine.

questions.prompt: Selection is finished and a hyperparameter value has been chosen. What data should the final model be refitted on before it is measured on the test set?
options: All of the training data, including the part held out as validation
Only the portion used for training during selection
The validation set
The test set
questions.explanation: The validation split has done its job once selection is over, so the final model may as well learn from it too — more data, better model. The test set is still never trained on.

questions.prompt: A decision tree is grown with `max_leaf_nodes = 8`. What is the minimum possible depth of such a tree, and why is the actual tree usually deeper?
questions.answer:
A **perfectly balanced** binary tree with 8 leaves has depth **3**, since 2³ = 8.

The actual tree is usually **deeper**, because splitting is greedy and driven by impurity, not by balance. It will happily split one branch repeatedly while leaving another as a leaf, producing a lopsided tree with the same 8 leaves but a longer deepest path.

questions.prompt: A perfectly balanced binary tree has {{leaves}} leaves. What is its depth?

steps.text: A balanced binary tree of depth d has 2^d leaves.
So `d = log₂({{leaves}})`.
`= {{log2(leaves)}}`

questions.explanation: This is the **minimum** depth for that many leaves. A greedy tree is usually deeper because it splits unevenly.

questions.prompt: Why is the split at the root of a decision tree the most influential one?
questions.answer:
Because the root split applies to **every example**. It is chosen as the single split that most reduces impurity across the whole dataset, and everything below it is conditioned on it.

A split deep in the tree affects only the small subset that reaches that node, so however good it is locally, it changes far fewer predictions.

questions.prompt: What does an internal decision node of a fitted tree represent, and how should it be described?
questions.answer:
In terms of the **data, not the code**. A node reading `Elevation <= 3044.5` means:

'Of the examples reaching this node, those with elevation at or below 3044.5 m go left and the rest go right. That threshold was chosen because splitting there most reduces impurity at this node — cover types at low elevation differ systematically from those higher up.'

So: name the feature, the threshold, which way each branch goes, and **what it means about the problem**. A description that only restates the syntax has said nothing.

questions.prompt: Train and test data arrive as two separate files. You split the training file 80/20. What is the 20% part?
options: A validation set
A second test set
Data that must not be used at all
A cross-validation fold
questions.explanation: The test set already exists as its own file, so a split inside the training data can only produce a **validation** set — the part you are allowed to select on. Calling it a test set is the mistake that leads to selecting on test.

questions.prompt: Raising `max_leaf_nodes` makes the tree more complex, which lowers its {{1}} and raises its {{2}}.
questions.explanation: More leaves means more, smaller regions: better able to fit the real structure, and better able to fit the noise along with it.

questions.prompt: Repeating a train/validation split many times and aggregating lets you report which of these?
options: The mean accuracy of each setting
How variable each setting is across splits
The shape of each setting's accuracy distribution
An unbiased estimate of performance on unseen data
questions.explanation: The last is what the **test set** is for. Repeating splits inside the training data tells you how a setting behaves under resampling, not how it will do on data nobody has touched.

subtopics.title: Feature subsets and reading coefficients
subtopics.summary: Exhaustive subset search, and the trap in reading logistic regression coefficients as feature importance.

questions.prompt: An exhaustive search fits a model on every non-empty subset of {{f}} features. How many fits is that?

steps.text: Each feature is either in or out, giving `2^f` subsets in total.
Excluding the empty subset: `{{2^f}} − 1 = {{n}}`

questions.explanation: With 9 features that is 2⁹ − 1 = **511** models — cheap. With 30 it is over a billion, which is why exhaustive search is only ever available on small feature sets.

questions.prompt: With 9 features, how many subsets contain exactly k features, for k = 1 … 8? What does that pattern imply when you plot performance against subset size?
questions.answer:
The binomial coefficients `C(9, k)`:

| k | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| count | 9 | 36 | 84 | 126 | 126 | 84 | 36 | 9 |

They are **symmetric** and **peak in the middle**. So a plot against subset size has far more observations at sizes 4 and 5 than at 1 or 8 — the extreme columns summarise only nine subsets each, and their shape is correspondingly unreliable. Any conclusion drawn from the ends of that plot deserves less confidence than one drawn from the middle.

questions.prompt: A dataset has {{f}} features. How many subsets leave out exactly one feature?

steps.text: A subset of size `f − 1` is determined entirely by the single feature it **excludes**.
There are `f` features that could be the one left out.
So there are `{{f}}` such subsets — the same count as the single-feature subsets.

questions.explanation: Choosing what to include and choosing what to exclude are the same decision, which is why C(n, k) = C(n, n−k). Both ends of a subset sweep are therefore narrow; the count peaks in the middle.

questions.prompt: What relationship would you expect between feature-subset size and validation accuracy, and why?
questions.answer:
Accuracy **rises steeply** from one feature to about three or four, then **plateaus**, with the spread narrowing as subsets grow.

Why: the first few informative features carry most of the signal. Beyond that, extra features add little — predictors in real data are usually correlated, so the fifth largely repeats what the first four already said.

The **spread** matters as much as the mean: small subsets vary enormously depending on *which* features they contain, while large subsets are all much the same because they all contain the good ones.

questions.prompt: Why is a violin plot a good choice for showing performance against feature-subset size?
questions.answer:
At each subset size there are **many** subsets — 126 of size 4, for instance — so the data at each x is a distribution, not a point.

A violin plot shows that distribution: the **spread** across subsets of the same size, and where the density lies. A line of means would hide the most interesting finding, which is that **small subsets vary hugely** in quality while large ones do not.

A scatter would also show spread, but with hundreds of overlapping points; a box plot shows quartiles but not shape.

questions.prompt: Are logistic regression coefficient magnitudes a reliable indicator of feature importance?
questions.answer:
**Only under conditions**, and even then with care.

The headline problem is **scale**: a coefficient is per unit of its feature, so a feature measured in small units gets a large coefficient for the same real effect. Comparing magnitudes is meaningless unless the features are **standardised first** — which is one reason a `StandardScaler` belongs in the pipeline.

Even when scaled, they mislead if features are **correlated**: two features carrying the same information can split the weight between them, or take large opposing coefficients that mostly cancel. Neither looks like its true importance.

questions.prompt: Why must features be standardised before comparing logistic regression coefficients?
options: A coefficient is per unit of its feature, so unit choice changes its size
Logistic regression cannot fit unscaled data
Standardisation makes all coefficients positive
Otherwise the coefficients cannot be computed
questions.explanation: Measure a length in metres rather than millimetres and its coefficient grows a thousandfold, without anything about the underlying relationship changing.

questions.prompt: Give a situation where selecting features solely by coefficient magnitude would perform poorly.
questions.answer:
**Correlated features.** Suppose two features are near-duplicates and jointly important. Logistic regression may split the weight between them, giving each a middling coefficient — so a magnitude ranking drops both, discarding information that was actually essential.

The reverse also occurs: two correlated features can take **large coefficients with opposite signs** that largely cancel. Both look critical by magnitude, but removing either barely changes predictions.

Correlated predictors are the norm in real data, so this is the live case rather than a hypothetical. The honest check is to refit without the feature and see whether performance moves.

questions.prompt: You want the four most influential features from a fitted logistic regression. On what should the coefficients be ranked?
options: Absolute value — a large negative coefficient is as influential as a large positive one
The raw signed coefficient, descending
p-value
The order the features appear in
questions.explanation: Rank on magnitude, because sign is direction rather than strength. Sorting the signed values would put every negative coefficient at the bottom regardless of how strong it is.

questions.prompt: What does the sign of a logistic regression coefficient mean?
questions.answer:
A **positive** coefficient means that increasing the feature increases `xᵀθ`, and so increases the predicted probability of the **positive class**.

A **negative** one pushes the prediction toward class 0.

Magnitude gives strength, sign gives direction — which is why importance is ranked on the absolute value, not on the signed coefficient.

questions.prompt: How should you judge whether an added modelling complication — polynomial features, say — was worthwhile?
questions.answer:
By comparing the accuracy **gain** against the cost, in the units of the experiment.

When a baseline already scores in the high 90s, the headroom is a percentage point or two. A gain of 0.3% on a validation set of ~137 rows is **less than one example** — well inside the noise, and not evidence of anything.

Against that, polynomial features multiply the feature count, the fit time and the overfitting risk. So the honest answer is often **no**, and saying so with the numbers behind it is worth more than claiming an improvement the data does not support.

questions.prompt: Hundreds of candidate models are compared on a single validation set. How well should the winner's validation score predict its test score?
questions.answer:
**Worse than you would expect**, and predictably in one direction.

With hundreds of candidates evaluated on one sample, the winner is partly a **selection artefact**: try enough candidates and one will look good by luck. Its test accuracy is usually **lower** than its validation accuracy, and that gap is the honest finding rather than an error.

That is the multiple-comparisons version of the argument for quarantining the test set — and the reason to record both numbers for every candidate, so the size of the gap can be seen.
questions.source: Lab 3 · Parts A, C; intro · slide 30

questions.prompt: Why might `LogisticRegression` need `max_iter` raised above its default?
options: The default iteration limit can be reached before the solver converges
It makes the model more accurate
It is required when using a Pipeline
It sets the number of feature subsets
questions.explanation: Logistic regression has no closed form and is solved iteratively; hitting the cap produces a convergence warning and a not-quite-fitted model. Scaling the features first usually reduces the iterations needed.

questions.prompt: Both validation and test accuracy are recorded for every candidate model. Which may be used to pick the winner, and why?
options: Validation — selecting on test accuracy would invalidate the test set as an estimate
Test — it is the more realistic measurement
Whichever is higher for the model you prefer
Both, averaged together
questions.explanation: Both are recorded, but only validation may be used to *choose*. Test is recorded so that afterwards you can report what the chosen model actually achieves.

questions.prompt: Coefficient magnitudes only compare across features once those features have been {{1}}, and even then they mislead when the features are {{2}}.
questions.explanation: Scale is the obvious trap and correlation is the subtle one: correlated predictors can split a shared effect between them, or take large opposing coefficients that cancel.

questions.prompt: Exhaustive feature-subset search is a defensible method when which of these hold?
options: The feature count is small enough that 2ⁿ − 1 fits is affordable
Each individual fit is cheap
The winner is chosen on validation data, not test data
You need a guarantee that the winning subset will generalise
questions.explanation: No search gives the fourth. Comparing hundreds of candidates on one validation sample is a multiple-comparisons problem — the winner's validation score is optimistic, which is exactly why its test score has to be reported separately.

keyFacts.definition: Fitting a model on every non-empty subset of n features means 2ⁿ − 1 fits. Feasible at n = 9 (511 models); hopeless by n = 30.
A coefficient is per unit of its feature, so magnitudes only compare after standardisation — and even then correlated features can split or cancel weight, making magnitude a weak importance signal.

subtopics.title: Reading experimental results
subtopics.summary: The interpretation skills all three labs mark on: telling a real difference from noise, and saying what a plot does and does not show.

questions.prompt: Two settings score 96.4% and 96.7% on a validation set of 137 examples. Is that a real difference?
questions.answer:
Almost certainly **not**. 0.3% of 137 examples is **0.4 of one example** — the two models differ on essentially no predictions, and reordering a single borderline case would flip which one wins.

The right response is to treat them as **tied** and choose on other grounds: simplicity, stability across splits, or interpretability. Reporting the 96.7% model as 'best' overstates what the experiment showed.

questions.prompt: A validation set has {{n}} examples. An accuracy difference of {{d}} percentage points corresponds to how many examples? Give it to 2 dp.

steps.text: A percentage point is 1/100 of the examples.
`= {{ex | 2}}` examples.

questions.explanation: Worth doing before calling any difference meaningful — on a small validation set, a percentage point can be a single example.

questions.prompt: Setting A has mean accuracy 0.842 with standard deviation 0.004; setting B has mean 0.847 with standard deviation 0.021. Which would you choose?
questions.answer:
Arguably **A**, despite the lower mean.

B's advantage is 0.005 while its standard deviation is 0.021 — the gap is about a **quarter of one standard deviation**, so on any given split B could easily do worse. A is far more **predictable**.

This is exactly the judgement a stability analysis exists to support: the mean alone would have picked B without noticing the risk.

questions.prompt: What does the validation accuracy curve look like as tree complexity increases, and where is the best setting?
questions.answer:
It **rises steeply** as the tree gains enough capacity to capture real structure, reaches a **plateau or gentle peak**, and then **declines or flattens** as the extra leaves start fitting noise.

The best setting sits at the top of that curve — often at the **start** of the plateau rather than its exact maximum, since the simplest model within the plateau is the more defensible choice.

The same U-shape as c4's error-versus-complexity plot, measured rather than drawn.

questions.prompt: Several settings sit on a flat plateau of near-identical accuracy. Which should you choose?
options: The simplest one on the plateau
The most complex one, since it has the most capacity
The one with the single highest mean, regardless of spread
The one at the middle of the range
questions.explanation: Equal performance for less complexity: cheaper, more stable across splits, and more interpretable. Chasing the exact maximum is fitting the validation noise.

questions.prompt: Your chosen model scores 97.8% on validation and 95.6% on test. Is something wrong?
questions.answer:
Not necessarily — this is the **expected** direction.

The model was **chosen** on validation, so that score is optimistic: among many candidates, the winner is partly winning on that sample's quirks. The test score, measured once on data used for nothing else, is the honest number.

It is worth reporting the gap rather than hiding it, and the **test** figure is the one to quote as the model's performance.

questions.prompt: Why read a per-class classification report rather than overall accuracy alone?
questions.answer:
Accuracy hides **which** class the errors fall on. When one class outnumbers the other, a classifier can score well overall while doing noticeably worse on the minority class specifically — and that is usually the class you care about.

The **classification report** breaks precision, recall and F1 down per class, so a high overall accuracy sitting next to a low recall on the important class is immediately visible.

questions.prompt: A classification report already gives precision, recall and F1 per class. What does a confusion matrix add?
options: The raw counts, showing exactly how many errors of each kind occurred
The per-class precision and recall
The overall accuracy
Nothing — it is redundant
questions.explanation: The report gives rates; the matrix gives counts. '3 malignant cases missed' lands differently from 'recall 0.94', and on a small test set the counts are what make the rates concrete.

questions.prompt: An accuracy plot sets `plt.ylim(0.90, 1.00)` because every value sits above 0.90. What does that gain, and what caveat comes with it?
questions.answer:
**Gain:** on a full 0–1 axis the values would be compressed into a flat line at the top. Zooming makes the differences between settings visible at all.

**Caveat:** it also **exaggerates** them visually. A drop that looks dramatic on a 0.90–1.00 axis may be a fraction of a percent — a handful of examples. The axis range should be stated whenever the plot is discussed, so the reader can calibrate what they are looking at.

questions.prompt: Which of these should be stated when presenting an accuracy plot?
options: The y-axis range, when it has been truncated
Whether the numbers are validation or test scores
How many examples the accuracies were measured on
The wall-clock time each fit took
questions.explanation: Each of the three is needed to calibrate what the reader is looking at: a truncated axis exaggerates differences, validation scores are optimistic, and a small evaluation set makes a percentage point a handful of examples.

questions.prompt: Before calling a small accuracy difference real, what should you convert it into?
questions.hint: Turn the percentage back into the thing it was a percentage of.
questions.explanation: 0.3% of a 137-row validation set is 0.4 of one example — the two models disagree on essentially no predictions. Percentages hide how few decisions the comparison rests on; counts do not.
